newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Collor wants another chance at Brazil presidency.
newsitem.headline: Collor wants another chance at Brazil presidency.

text.p: Former Brazilian President Fernando Collor, who was forced to resign amid a corruption scandal in 1992, said in an interview published on Sunday that he would return to Brazil and run for president next year.
Collor, who lives in self-imposed exile in Miami, told news magazine Veja he would soon be spending more time in Brazil than in the United States to prepare for the 1998 election.
"I feel I was impeded from finishing something very important ... I can't say that I feel like an accomplished man," Collor, 47, told Veja.
"I think that can only happen if I ... have the chance to run for office again and submit myself to the popular will," he said.
The Supreme Court cleared Collor of corruption charges in 1994, but he remains banned from holding office until 2002.

Collor said he would be travelling to Brazil beginning in August. Accompanying him will be a team of attorneys who he hopes can reverse the ban on holding office. If they do not succeed, Collor says he will be back in 2002.
"This return to the polls is something that is going to happen, whether my opponents want it or not," he told Veja.

The youthful-looking former leader told the magazine he spends much of his spare time on the tennis court or playing backgammon on the Internet with opponents in the United Arab Emirates, Brazil and elsewhere in the world.
Although Collor in the past has talked about returning home to run for president and clear his name, he has never been so specific about his plans.
He gave the current administration of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso a performance rating of five on a scale of one to 10.

Political analysts, however, give the disgraced former president next-to-nothing odds of unseating Cardoso, father of a successful inflation-fighting plan that has given the Brazilian economy a stability it has not seen since the 1970s.
Cardoso recently pushed a constitutional amendment through Congress that allows him to run for an unprecedented second term.
